title: Reduced monomial basis of a monomial minus scalar quotient
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbf N^n\setminus\{0\}$, and $c\in A$. Put $P=A[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], $X^a=\prod_iX_i^{a_i}$, and $C=P/(X^a-c)$. Let $E_a=\{b\in\mathbf N^n:\text{there exists }i\text{ with }b_i<a_i\}$. Then the family $(\overline{X^b})_{b\in E_a}$ is an $A$-module basis of $C$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module]: every element of $C$ has a unique expression $\sum_{b\in E_a}u_b\overline{X^b}$ with $u_b\in A$ and only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Zero entries of $a$, zero or invertible $c$, and rings with zero divisors are allowed.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), printed pp.250--251, exercise: agent-supplied general algebra input for the monomial presentation of Definition 3.5.11; the general basis assertion is an agent generalization, not a verbatim lemma of ILO. Its independent coefficient-reduction argument is recorded in report.md.

proof.text: For $v\in\mathbf N^n$, let $q(v)$ be the largest $q\in\mathbf N$ with $qa\leq v$ coordinatewise. This exists: $0$ is allowed, and choosing $j$ with $a_j>0$ bounds $q\leq v_j$. Put $b(v)=v-q(v)a$. Then $b(v)\geq0$ and $b(v)\in E_a$, since otherwise $(q(v)+1)a\leq v$. Conversely, if $v=b+qa$ with $b\in E_a$, choose $i$ with $b_i<a_i$; then $a_i>0$ and $(q+1)a_i>v_i$, so $q=q(v)$ and $b=b(v)$. Applying this uniqueness to $v+a=b(v)+(q(v)+1)a$ gives $q(v+a)=q(v)+1$ and $b(v+a)=b(v)$. In particular $v\in E_a$ gives $q(v)=0$ and $b(v)=v$.

source.place: Expose XVI Definition 3.5.11 and Lemma 3.5.13(i), printed pp.250--251: agent coefficient-reduction argument for the general algebra input; the general basis assertion and this proof are not asserted verbatim in ILO.

proof.text: Let $V\subset P$ be the $A$-submodule of polynomials supported in $E_a$. By the finite coefficient description of the polynomial ring, define $N:P\to V$ by $N(\sum_v u_vX^v)=\sum_v u_vc^{q(v)}X^{b(v)}$. This is a finite sum, supported on the image of the finite support of the input. Coefficientwise addition and scalar multiplication show directly that $N$ is $A$-linear. The last assertion of step 1 gives $N(h)=h$ for $h\in V$.

source.place: Expose XVI Definition 3.5.11 and Lemma 3.5.13(i), printed pp.250--251: agent coefficient-reduction argument for the general algebra input; the general basis assertion and this proof are not asserted verbatim in ILO.

proof.text: Write $f=X^a-c$ and $I=(f)=\{fg:g\in P\}$; this set is an ideal, since sums and products with arbitrary elements remain multiples of $f$, and it is the smallest ideal containing $f$. On each monomial the formulas of step 1 give $N(X^aX^v)=c^{q(v)+1}X^{b(v)}=cN(X^v)$. Expanding a finite polynomial and using linearity therefore gives $N(fg)=0$ for every $g\in P$. Thus $N$ kills $I$. The quotient map $\pi:P\to C$ is surjective with kernel $I$, so if $\pi(h)=\pi(h\prime)$ then $N(h)=N(h\prime)$.

source.place: Expose XVI Definition 3.5.11 and Lemma 3.5.13(i), printed pp.250--251: agent coefficient-reduction argument for the general algebra input; the general basis assertion and this proof are not asserted verbatim in ILO.

proof.text: For $v=b+qa$ as in step 1, if $q=0$ then $X^v-N(X^v)=0$. If $q>0$, cancellation of consecutive terms in the finite sum gives $(T-c)\sum_{r=0}^{q-1}T^{q-1-r}c^r=T^q-c^q$. Substituting $T=X^a$ and multiplying by $X^b$ yields $X^v-N(X^v)=(X^a-c)X^b\sum_{r=0}^{q-1}(X^a)^{q-1-r}c^r\in I$. Sum with the coefficients of any $h\in P$ to obtain $h-N(h)\in I$. Hence $\pi(h)=\pi(N(h))$; surjectivity of $\pi$ proves existence of the required finite reduced expression in $C$.

source.place: Expose XVI Definition 3.5.11 and Lemma 3.5.13(i), printed pp.250--251: agent coefficient-reduction argument for the general algebra input; the general basis assertion and this proof are not asserted verbatim in ILO.

proof.text: If $h,h\prime\in V$ give two reduced expressions for the same element of $C$, step 3 gives $N(h-h\prime)=0$. Step 2 gives $N(h-h\prime)=h-h\prime$, so $h=h\prime$. Equality in the polynomial ring is coefficientwise, so the two finitely supported coefficient families on $E_a$ agree. Together with existence from step 4, this is exactly the basis property. The argument only uses $a\ne0$ to bound the integer in step 1; it never divides by $c$ or cancels a nonzero ring element. Thus it applies also to zero entries of $a$, $c=0$, units $c$, the zero ring, and rings with zero divisors.
